questions.title: GATE CSE 2006 | Question: 25
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Let $S = \{1, 2, 3,\ldots, m\}, m >3.$ Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be subsets of $S$ each of size $3.$ Define a function $f$ from $S$ to the set of natural numbers as, $f(i)$ is the number of sets $X_j$ that contain the element $i.$ That is $f(i)=\left | \left\{j \mid i\in X_j \right\} \right|$   then $ \sum_{i=1}^{m} f(i)$ is:

  1. $3m$
  2. $3n$
  3. $2m+1$
  4. $2n+1$

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key cross-checked against the GateOverflow question and an independent derivation; the historical index lists no official key for these years.
review.independentCheck: Double-count incidences (i,j) with i in X_j; each of n size-3 sets contributes exactly three.
review.notes: Double-count incidences (i,j) with i in X_j; each of n size-3 sets contributes exactly three.

questions.title: GATE IT 2006 | Question: 26
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
What are the eigenvalues of the matrix $P$ given below

$$P= \begin{pmatrix} a &1 &0 \\ 1& a& 1\\ 0&1 &a \end{pmatrix}$$                               

  1. $a, a -√2, a + √2$
  2. $a, a, a$
  3. $0, a, 2a$
  4. $-a, 2a, 2a$

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key cross-checked against the GateOverflow question and an independent derivation; the historical index lists no official key for these years.
review.independentCheck: Write P=aI+T; the path-three adjacency matrix T has characteristic polynomial lambda(lambda^2-2).
review.notes: Write P=aI+T; the path-three adjacency matrix T has characteristic polynomial lambda(lambda^2-2).

questions.title: GATE CSE 2006 | Question: 26
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Which one of the first order predicate calculus statements given below correctly expresses the following English statement?

 Tigers and lions attack if they are hungry or threatened.

  1. $∀x[(\text{tiger}(x) ∧ \text{lion}(x)) → {(\text{hungry}(x) ∨ \text{threatened}(x)) → \text{attacks}(x)}]$
  2. $∀x[(\text{tiger}(x) ∨ \text{lion}(x)) → {(\text{hungry}(x) ∨ \text{threatened}(x)) ∧ \text{attacks}(x)}]$
  3. $∀x[(\text{tiger}(x) ∨ \text{lion}(x)) → {\text{attacks}(x) → (\text{hungry}(x) ∨ \text{threatened}(x))}]$
  4. $∀x[(\text{tiger}(x) ∨ \text{lion}(x)) → {(\text{hungry}(x) ∨ \text{threatened}(x)) → \text{attacks}(x)}]$

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key cross-checked against the GateOverflow question and an independent derivation; the historical index lists no official key for these years.
review.independentCheck: Translate the subject as tiger OR lion and the sufficient condition as hungry OR threatened implies attacks.
review.notes: Translate the subject as tiger OR lion and the sufficient condition as hungry OR threatened implies attacks.

questions.title: GATE IT 2006 | Question: 27
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Match the following iterative methods for solving algebraic equations and their orders of convergence.

  Method   Order of Convergence
1. Bisection P. 2 or more
2. Newton-Raphson Q. 1.62
3. Secant R. 1
4. Regula falsi S. 1 bit per iteration
  1. I-R, II-S, III-P, IV-Q
  2. I-S, II-R, III-Q, IV-P
  3. I-S, II-Q, III-R, IV-P
  4. I-S, II-P, III-Q, IV-R

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key cross-checked against the GateOverflow question and an independent derivation; the historical index lists no official key for these years.
review.independentCheck: Bisection is linear/one bit, Newton is quadratic, secant has order about 1.62, and regula falsi is linear.
review.notes: Bisection is linear/one bit, Newton is quadratic, secant has order about 1.62, and regula falsi is linear.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2006 | Question: 27
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following propositional statements:

  • $P_1: ((A ∧ B) → C)) ≡ ((A → C) ∧ (B → C))$
  • $P_2: ((A ∨ B) → C)) ≡ ((A → C) ∨ (B → C))$


Which one of the following is true?

  1. $P_1$ is a tautology, but not $P_2$
  2. $P_2$ is a tautology, but not $P_1$
  3. $P_1$ and $P_2$ are both tautologies
  4. Both $P_1$ and $P_2$ are not tautologies

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key cross-checked against the GateOverflow question and an independent derivation; the historical index lists no official key for these years.
review.independentCheck: A=T,B=F,C=F is a counterexample to each displayed equivalence, so neither is a tautology.
review.notes: A=T,B=F,C=F is a counterexample to each displayed equivalence, so neither is a tautology.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2006 | Question: 28
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
A logical binary relation $\odot$, is defined as follows: 

$$\begin{array}{|l|l|l|} \hline \textbf{A} & \textbf{B}& \textbf{A} \odot \textbf{B}\\\hline \text{True} & \text{True}& \text{True}\\\hline \text{True} & \text{False}& \text{True}\\\hline \text{False} & \text{True}& \text{False}\\\hline \text{False} & \text{False}& \text{True}\\\hline   \end{array}$$

Let $\sim$ be the unary negation (NOT) operator, with higher precedence then $\odot$.

Which one of the following is equivalent to $A\wedge B$ ?

  1. $(\sim A\odot B)$
  2. $\sim(A \odot \sim B)$
  3. $\sim(\sim A\odot\sim B)$
  4. $\sim(\sim A\odot B)$

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key cross-checked against the GateOverflow question and an independent derivation; the historical index lists no official key for these years.
review.independentCheck: The truth table is A OR NOT B; option D negates (NOT A OR NOT B) to obtain A AND B.
review.notes: The truth table is A OR NOT B; option D negates (NOT A OR NOT B) to obtain A AND B.

questions.title: GATE IT 2006 | Question: 65
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
In the 4B/5B encoding scheme, every 4 bits of data are encoded in a 5-bit codeword.
It is required that the codewords have at most 1 leading and at most 1 trailing zero.
How many are such codewords possible?

  1. 14
  2. 16
  3. 18
  4. 20

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key cross-checked against the GateOverflow question and an independent derivation; the historical index lists no official key for these years.
review.independentCheck: Partition the 5-bit strings by first/last bit; the valid counts are 8, 4, 4, and 2, totaling 18.
review.notes: Partition the 5-bit strings by first/last bit; the valid counts are 8, 4, 4, and 2, totaling 18.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2006 | Question: 71
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
The $2^n$  vertices of a graph $G$ corresponds to all subsets of a set of size $n$, for $n \geq 6$.  Two vertices of $G$ are adjacent if and only if the corresponding sets intersect in exactly two elements.
The number of vertices of degree zero in $G$ is:

  1. $1$
  2. $n$
  3. $n + 1$
  4. $2^n$

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key cross-checked against the GateOverflow question and an independent derivation; the historical index lists no official key for these years.
review.independentCheck: Exactly the empty set and the n singletons have no 2-element intersection with any vertex.
review.notes: Exactly the empty set and the n singletons have no 2-element intersection with any vertex.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2006 | Question: 72
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
The $2^n$  vertices of a graph $G$ corresponds to all subsets of a set of size $n$, for $n \geq 6$. Two vertices of $G$ are adjacent if and only if the corresponding sets intersect in exactly two elements.

The maximum degree of a vertex in $G$ is:

  1. $\binom{\frac{n}{2}}{2}.2^{\frac{n}{2}}$
  2. $2^{n-2}$
  3. $2^{n-3}\times 3$
  4. $2^{n-1}$

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key cross-checked against the GateOverflow question and an independent derivation; the historical index lists no official key for these years.
review.independentCheck: For |A|=k, degree is C(k,2)2^(n-k), maximized at k=3 or k=4.
review.notes: For |A|=k, degree is C(k,2)2^(n-k), maximized at k=3 or k=4.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2006 | Question: 73
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
The $2^n$  vertices of a graph $G$ corresponds to all subsets of a set of size $n$, for $n \geq 6$.  Two vertices of $G$ are adjacent if and only if the corresponding sets intersect in exactly two elements.

The number of connected components in $G$ is:

  1. $n$
  2. $n + 2$
  3. $2^{\frac{n}{2}}$
  4. $\frac{2^{n}}{n}$

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key cross-checked against the GateOverflow question and an independent derivation; the historical index lists no official key for these years.
review.independentCheck: The empty set and n singletons are isolated; all subsets of size at least two are connected through their 2-subsets.
review.notes: The empty set and n singletons are isolated; all subsets of size at least two are connected through their 2-subsets.

questions.title: GATE IT 2005 | Question: 1
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
A bag contains $10$ blue marbles, $20$ green marbles and $30$ red marbles. A marble is drawn from the bag, its colour recorded and it is put back in the bag. This process is repeated $3$ times. The probability that no two of the marbles drawn have the same colour is

  1. $\left(\dfrac{1}{36}\right)$
  2. $\left(\dfrac{1}{6}\right)$
  3. $\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)$
  4. $\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)$

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key cross-checked against the GateOverflow question and an independent derivation; the historical index lists no official key for these years.
review.independentCheck: Independence and six permutations give 6*(10/60)*(20/60)*(30/60)=1/6.
review.notes: Independence and six permutations give 6*(10/60)*(20/60)*(30/60)=1/6.

questions.title: GATE IT 2005 | Question: 2
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
If the trapezoidal method is used to evaluate the integral obtained $\int_{0}^{1} x^2dx$, then the value obtained

  1. is always > (1/3)
  2. is always < (1/3)
  3. is always = (1/3)
  4. may be greater or lesser than (1/3)

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key cross-checked against the GateOverflow question and an independent derivation; the historical index lists no official key for these years.
review.independentCheck: Strict convexity makes every trapezoidal chord lie above x^2, so the composite estimate exceeds the integral.
review.notes: Strict convexity makes every trapezoidal chord lie above x^2, so the composite estimate exceeds the integral.

questions.title: GATE IT 2005 | Question: 3
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
The determinant of the matrix given below is

$$\begin{bmatrix}
0 &1  &0  &2 \\
 -1&  1&  1& 3\\
 0&0  &0  & 1\\
 1&  -2&  0& 1
\end{bmatrix}$$

  1. $-1$
  2. $0$
  3. $1$
  4. $2$

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key cross-checked against the GateOverflow question and an independent derivation; the historical index lists no official key for these years.
review.independentCheck: Cofactor expansion along row three gives minus the 3x3 minor, hence determinant -1.
review.notes: Cofactor expansion along row three gives minus the 3x3 minor, hence determinant -1.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2005 | Question: 7
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
The time complexity of computing the transitive closure of a binary relation on a set of $n$ elements is known to be:

  1. $O(n)$

  2. $O(n \log  n)$

  3. $O \left( n^{\frac{3}{2}} \right)$

review.notes: Warshall's standard Boolean-matrix recurrence performs n^2 updates for each of n intermediate vertices.

questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics

Let $A, B$ and $C$ be non-empty sets and let $X = ( A - B ) - C$ and $Y = ( A - C ) - ( B - C ).$ Which one of the following is TRUE?

  1. $X = Y$
  2. $X ⊂ Y$
  3. $Y ⊂ X$
  4. None of these

The poset is :

  1. not a lattice

questions.title: GATE CSE 2005 | Question: 10
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Let $G$ be a simple connected planar graph with $13$ vertices and $19$ edges. Then, the number of faces in the planar embedding of the graph is:

  1. $6$

questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Let $G$ be a simple graph with $20$ vertices and $100$ edges. The size of the minimum vertex cover of G is $8$. Then, the size of the maximum independent set of $G$ is:

questions.title: GATE CSE 2005 | Question: 12, ISRO2009-64
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Let $f(x)$ be the continuous probability density function of a random variable $x$, the probability that $a < x \leq b$, is :

  1. $f(b-a)$
  2. $f(b) - f(a)$
  3. $\int\limits_a^b f(x) dx$
  4. $\int\limits_a^b xf (x)dx$

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key cross-checked against the GateOverflow question and an independent derivation; the historical index lists no official key for these years.
review.independentCheck: For a continuous density, interval probability is the integral of the density over that interval.
review.notes: For a continuous density, interval probability is the integral of the density over that interval.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2005 | Question: 13
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
The set \(\{1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 11, 13, 14\}\) is a group under multiplication modulo $15$. The inverses of $4$ and $7$ are respectively:

  1. $3$ and $13$
  2. $2$ and $11$

  4. $8$ and $14$

review.notes: 4*4 is 1 modulo 15 and 7*13 is 1 modulo 15.

questions.title: GATE IT 2005 | Question: 31
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Let $f$ be a function from a set $A$ to a set $B$, $g$ a function from $B$ to $C$, and $h$ a function from $A$ to $C$, such that $h(a) = g(f(a))$ for all $a ∈ A.$ Which of the following statements is always true for all such functions $f$ and $g$?

  1. $g$ is onto $\implies$ $h$ is onto
  2. $h$ is onto $\implies$ $f$ is onto
  3. $h$ is onto $\implies$ $g$ is onto
  4. $h$ is onto $\implies$ $f$ and $g$ are onto

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key cross-checked against the GateOverflow question and an independent derivation; the historical index lists no official key for these years.
review.independentCheck: Range(g composed with f) is a subset of range(g); surjectivity of the composition therefore forces g to be onto.
review.notes: Range(g composed with f) is a subset of range(g); surjectivity of the composition therefore forces g to be onto.
